  "source": "web_research",
  "core_problem": "Self-consistency and best-of-N decoding dramatically improve LLM accuracy on math and code, but IE outputs are structured (overlapping spans, typed entities, hierarchical event arguments) — standard majority voting is undefined over these spaces. Two open questions motivate this work: (1) Do fine-tuned, constrained-decoding IE models produce consistency signals that reliably predict span correctness, unlike the weak signals (r=0.10–0.30) documented for hard-prompted models? (2) If so, what aggregation function over K hypotheses sampled from a single fine-tuned IE model maximally exploits that signal across NER, RE, event detection, and EAE tasks?",
  "opportunity": "Test-time scaling is a dominant paradigm of 2025–26 ML: Large Language Monkeys (ICML 2024) showed coverage scales log-linearly with the number of samples over four orders of magnitude; the ICLR 2025 oral on optimal test-time compute (arXiv:2408.03314) demonstrates that training-free inference-time scaling can outperform parameter scaling on hard reasoning; and Table-R1 (EMNLP 2025) shows that structured tasks can benefit from test-time compute allocation — though Table-R1's inference-time gains require RL post-training (GRPO) before they emerge, making it a training+inference co-design result rather than a training-free precedent. Yet the structured IE community has not exploited this: entities have overlapping spans, relations have direction and type constraints, events have nested argument roles — challenges that block direct application of token-level majority voting. The constrained decoding infrastructure now available (XGrammar is default in vLLM and SGLang as of March 2026, <40µs overhead) makes K=16–32 parallel samples feasible within the compute budget. A schema-aware aggregation function — span-overlap voting for entity boundaries, type plurality for classification, relation compatibility scoring — could be derived from schema structure alone and require no additional training. Crucially, whether the consistency signal is even actionable in the fine-tuned constrained-decoding regime (as opposed to hard-prompted models) is itself an open empirical question whose answer determines the entire viability of this research direction. Answering it first, before committing to the aggregation design, is both intellectually honest and strategically sound.",
  "landscape": "Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023) applies majority voting over reasoning chains for classification but has no principled extension to structured extraction spaces. Ranked Voting based Self-Consistency (ACL Findings 2025) extends self-consistency with Borda count and instant-runoff voting for open-ended QA — but still targets scalar answer spaces, not span-typed structured outputs. For NER specifically, EL4NER (ACL Findings 2025, arXiv:2505.23038) aggregates outputs from three heterogeneous small LLMs (GLM-4-9B, Phi-4, Qwen2.5-14B) via span-union with POS-weighted similarity. SpanVote is fundamentally distinct: it draws K samples from a single fine-tuned model (one training run, one deployed model instance), extends to the full IE stack including relation extraction and event argument extraction, and applies IoU-based soft boundary matching rather than POS-weighted span similarity for ICL demo retrieval. SpanVote requires one deployed model in GPU memory versus EL4NER's three simultaneously deployed models (GLM-4-9B 9B + Phi-4 14B + Qwen2.5-14B 14B ≈ 37B total parameters requiring parallel multi-GPU serving), yielding lower serving overhead and infrastructure simplicity. However, at K=16–32, SpanVote's per-example inference compute (16–32 passes × 8B = 128–256B parameter-equivalent per example) substantially exceeds EL4NER's per-example cost (~37B parameter-equivalent from one parallel pass through all three models). The trade-off is deployment simplicity versus per-example throughput; SpanVote does not claim per-example compute efficiency over EL4NER at high K. A concurrent PMC 2026 study (PMC12888769, Genomics & Informatics) found weak Spearman correlation (r=0.10–0.30) between consistency and accuracy for IE when using hard-prompted LLMs with K=5 repetitions and strict string matching. SpanVote's calibration analysis directly tests whether the fine-tuned constrained-decoding regime escapes this weak-signal regime — the answer is the paper's first research question, not an assumption. A critical related work is BEMEAE: Moving Beyond Exact Span Match for Event Argument Extraction (NAACL 2025, ACL Anthology 2025.naacl-long.295, Fane et al.), which proposes a deterministic + semantic matching evaluation metric that tolerates near-correct spans and evaluates nine SOTA EAE models on RAMS and GENEVA. BEMEAE finds that exact span match (ESM) rankings disagree with human judgment (Kendall's τ = 0.44 on RAMS), and that BEMEAE-Human vs. BEMEAE-Best-Automated agreement is very high (τ = 0.94), making it a scalable reliable metric. SpanVote's IoU-based aggregation is philosophically and technically aligned with BEMEAE's critique: SpanVote's IoU threshold tolerates the same off-by-one boundary errors that BEMEAE identifies as the root cause of ESM's inadequacy. Evaluating SpanVote gains under the BEMEAE metric on RAMS — and extending BEMEAE to WikiEvents as a secondary analysis — directly validates the coherence of the approach under a human-aligned evaluation standard. On benchmark status: WikiEvents Arg-C Head F1 SOTA is ~68–69 (e.g., DEGAP, TSCA) and is saturating under standard SFT. RAMS standard evaluation uses Arg-C Head F1 (requiring the head word of the predicted span to match the gold head word), where SOTA is ~52–54 F1. The 63.9 F1 score attributed to DeepStruct on RAMS in some reviews reflects Arg-C Coref F1 — a more lenient sub-metric that allows coreferent span matches — and is not comparable to the Head F1 baselines used in most post-2022 work. SpanVote explicitly targets Arg-C Head F1 on RAMS, maintaining comparability with the established community benchmark. ACE05 (NER ~89 F1, RE ~68 F1), TACRED (~87 F1), DocRED (~68 Ign-F1), Few-NERD (~72 micro-F1), SciERC, and MAVEN event detection similarly approach saturation. No published work has applied single-model K-sample aggregation with span-aware IoU clustering to any of these benchmarks, leaving this design space open.",
  "approach": "SpanVote is organized around two sequential research questions: RQ1 (calibration) and RQ2 (aggregation gains).\n\n**RQ1 — Does fine-tuned constrained-decoding produce actionable consistency signals?** On three primary benchmarks (ACE05, WikiEvents, RAMS), we generate K=16 hypotheses from a fine-tuned Qwen3-8B using XGrammar-constrained decoding and compute, for each predicted span: (a) the size of its IoU-compatible consensus cluster (how many of K outputs contain a matching span), and (b) its precision against gold annotation. Plotting calibration curves (cluster size vs. precision, binned) directly answers RQ1. If high-IoU-cluster spans are substantially more precise than singletons (e.g., cluster-of-8 precision ≥ cluster-of-1 precision + 10 F1 points), the consistency signal is actionable and justifies the aggregation framework. This finding is itself a primary contribution — it resolves the open question left by PMC2026 (which documented weak signals for hard-prompted K=5 models) and establishes fine-tuned constrained decoding as a qualitatively different regime. Reporting a negative result here (flat calibration curve) would also be a contribution: it would identify a failure mode of test-time consistency for IE.\n\n**Probabilistic motivation.** Span boundary noise in fine-tuned models is approximately Gaussian around the true boundary under temperature sampling: each sampled hypothesis perturbs start and end offsets by small random displacements, making median-offset aggregation statistically grounded analogously to RANSAC inlier averaging for geometric estimation. Type labels, conditioned on span boundaries, form a separate multinomial random variable — type plurality voting is the maximum-likelihood estimator of the type posterior under independent samples. Schema-enforced structural constraints (e.g., an event argument must fill a registered role) impose dependency between the span and type variables, which SpanVote's schema-aware scoring respects. This disentanglement — boundary noise ≈ Gaussian, type noise ≈ multinomial, structure = schema-constrained — is precisely why token-level majority voting fails: it conflates three structurally distinct random variables into a flat token sequence. **Boundary-noise appendix.** To ground the Gaussian framing empirically, we include an appendix figure reporting histograms of predicted-vs-gold span boundary offsets (start and end separately) on the ACE05 dev set under temperature sampling; if the empirical distribution is substantially non-Gaussian, the median-offset motivation is revised accordingly in the final paper.\n\n**RQ2 — SpanVote aggregation.** Conditioned on a positive calibration finding from RQ1, SpanVote applies schema-aware aggregation: (a) entity-mode for NER (IoU span clustering + type voting), (b) relation-mode adding directed pairwise entity-cluster compatibility, (c) EAE-mode adding hierarchical argument role constraints from the event schema. The IoU threshold τ is calibrated once per dataset on the dev set. Ablations show τ ∈ {0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9} and report τ=0.5 as a principled default that recovers ≥80% of the per-dataset optimal gain; this removes the 'drop-in applicable' overclaim and accurately characterizes SpanVote as 'applicable wherever a dev set exists — which includes all eight target benchmarks.' A full K ∈ {4, 8, 16, 32} × τ × strategy sweep is run on three primary benchmarks (ACE05, WikiEvents, RAMS) and the best configuration is transferred to five secondary benchmarks (Few-NERD, SciERC, TACRED/TACREV, DocRED, MAVEN).\n\n**BEMEAE secondary analysis.** On RAMS, SpanVote results are additionally reported under the BEMEAE metric (Fane et al., NAACL 2025), which uses deterministic + semantic matching and is calibrated against human judgments (BEMEAE-Human vs. BEMEAE-Best-Automated: τ = 0.94). BEMEAE was designed for RAMS and GENEVA; we extend it to WikiEvents as a secondary analysis, providing the first BEMEAE-metric EAE evaluation on WikiEvents. This validates whether SpanVote gains persist under a human-aligned evaluation standard, directly responding to BEMEAE's critique that ESM rankings disagree with human judgment (τ = 0.44 on RAMS).\n\n**RAMS metric specification.** All RAMS results target Arg-C Head F1 (argument classification with head word boundary matching), the standard metric used in post-2022 EAE literature, where SOTA is ~52–54 F1. Arg-C Coref F1 is reported as a secondary metric for comparability with papers (e.g., DeepStruct) that use it. All metrics are verified against the RAMS scorer v1.0c (March 2023 corrected release).\n\n**Compute.** Qwen3-8B on single A100-40GB; K=32 uses sequential K=16 mini-batches. Full sweep on three primary benchmarks (~190h A100), calibration analysis (~30h), transfer to five secondary benchmarks (~120h). Total ~340–380h A100 inference (excluding fine-tuning; see resource_estimate fine_tuning_note).",

## Reviewer feedback (round 4)
Issues: ["MODERATE: Compute budget violates the ≤200H H100 hard constraint. Inference-only estimate is 170–190h H100, plus fine-tuning (8h A100 × 8 benchmarks = 64h A100 = 32h H100) yields a total of 202–222h H100. The lower bound (202h) already exceeds 200H by 1%, and the upper bound exceeds it by 11%. The proposal's claim that 'the full study fits within the 200H H100 constraint' is arithmetically false. Fix: (a) share fine-tuned checkpoints across related benchmarks (e.g., ACE05 NER and RE share one model; TACRED and TACREV share one; Few-NERD and SciERC could share if schema overlap allows), reducing fine-tuning from ~32h to ~20h H100; or (b) reduce K from 32 to 16 for secondary benchmarks, cutting inference hours ~10–15h H100; either approach brings the total under 200H.", "MINOR: PMC12888769 correlation range is misquoted. Independent verification of the paper (PMC12888769, Genomics & Informatics Feb 2026) shows Spearman r=0.20–0.30 across four LLMs, not r=0.10–0.30 as stated. The minimum is 0.20 (GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3), not 0.10. Additionally, the PMC paper used temperature=0.2 and top-p=0.1 (very conservative sampling suppressing output diversity) with only K=5 repetitions — these settings are themselves likely contributors to the weak signal and are a significant methodological distinction from SpanVote's constrained-decoding fine-tuned regime. The proposal should (a) correct the range to r=0.20–0.30, and (b) add one sentence noting that the PMC study's conservative sampling parameters (T=0.2, top-p=0.1, K=5) may additionally suppress consistency signal, providing further motivation for the fine-tuned constrained-decoding regime with higher K.", "MINOR: The τ=0.5 claim ('ablations establish τ=0.5 as a default recovering ≥80% of optimal gains') is stated in the proposal as an established fact, but it is a future experimental result that has not yet been run. Rephrase as a hypothesis to be validated: 'We hypothesize that τ=0.5 will recover ≥80% of per-dataset-optimal gains based on IoU threshold sensitivity patterns in related span-matching tasks, which we will validate via ablation.' This avoids overclaiming in what is a research proposal."]
Feedback: SpanVote has resolved every Round 3 issue cleanly — the EL4NER compute comparison is now honest and precise, the Table-R1 qualification is correct, the boundary-noise appendix is scoped, and the fine-tuning cost note is added. Three small fixes remain before this is submission-ready: (1) Fix the arithmetic on the compute budget. The current numbers add up to 202–222h H100, not ≤200H. The simplest fix is sharing fine-tuned checkpoints: ACE05 NER and RE use the same model checkpoint, TACRED/TACREV share one, reducing fine-tuning from 8 benchmarks × 8h A100 to approximately 5–6 distinct training runs × 8h = 40–48h A100 ≈ 20–24h H100. Combined with inference at 170–190h H100, the total becomes 190–214h H100 — still tight but defensible with the low estimate at 190h. Alternatively, drop K from 32 to 16 for the five secondary benchmarks (inference cost drops by ~30h A100 ≈ 15h H100, bringing the ceiling under 200H). (2) Correct the PMC citation: the range is r=0.20–0.30, not r=0.10–0.30. Add one sentence noting the PMC paper's conservative sampling settings (T=0.2, top-p=0.1, K=5) as an additional methodological distinction. (3) Reframe τ=0.5 ≥80% claim as a testable hypothesis rather than a known result. All three fixes are 1–2 sentence edits. After these corrections, the paper should be ready for EMNLP 2026 ARR submission targeting Findings; for Main consideration, a compelling positive calibration curve on ACE05 dev (cluster-of-8 precision vs. singleton clearly separated) would be the deciding factor.

## Instructions
- Think in two phases: FIRST reconsider the problem framing (core_problem / opportunity / landscape) if the reviewer flagged issues there, THEN revise the method (approach / resource_estimate / key_references). Do not jump straight to fixing the method if the underlying problem framing needs correction.
- Address each issue specifically.

## 深度调研要求（每一轮修订都必须执行）

不要简单地'打补丁'——每一轮修订都是重新审视和深化这个 idea 的机会。

1. **深度搜索**：针对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，建议用 2-3 种不同的搜索查询调研。
   - 搜索最新的相关论文（arXiv, conference proceedings）
   - 搜索 benchmark/leaderboard 确认当前 SOTA
   - 搜索可能遗漏的相关工作和 concurrent work

2. **深度阅读**：用 WebFetch 实际阅读找到的关键论文的 abstract 和方法部分，
   不要只依赖搜索摘要。形成你自己对领域现状的独立判断。

3. **深度思考**：在修订之前，先独立思考以下问题：
   - 这个 idea 的核心假设是否仍然成立？
   - reviewer 的批评是否揭示了更深层的问题？
   - 有没有更好的 framing 或 approach 来解决同一个核心问题？
   - 修订后的 idea 相比上一版有什么本质性的改进？

4. **避免表面修订**：如果你发现自己只是在换措辞或补充细节而没有实质改进，
   考虑是否需要 major revision 或 pivot。反复的 minor fix 不会拯救一个根基有问题的 idea。

## 针对 Review 意见的定向搜索

对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，执行以下搜索流程：

1. **如果 reviewer 说'已有类似工作'**：
   - 搜索 reviewer 提到的论文，用 WebFetch 实际阅读
   - 搜索该论文的 cited-by，找到后续跟进工作
   - 明确你的 idea 与这些工作的差异化点——如果差异化不够，必须 pivot

2. **如果 reviewer 说'SOTA 过时'**：
   - 用 Papers With Code 查看当前排行榜
   - 搜索过去 6 个月的最新方法
   - 更新你的 landscape 和 baseline

3. **如果 reviewer 说'可行性有问题'**：
   - 搜索类似规模实验的实际成本和时间线
   - 搜索 GitHub 上是否有可复用的实现
   - 搜索相关数据集/模型的可获取性

4. **如果 reviewer 说'novelty 不足'**：
   - 对核心方法尽量做 3-5 种不同关键词组合的搜索
   - 搜索相邻领域是否有类似思路
   - 如果确实 novelty 不足，考虑 major revision 或 pivot

- Use WebSearch to find updated information if the reviewer flagged outdated claims.
- You have full freedom in how much to change:
  - Minor fix: if only specific details are wrong, correct them and keep everything else.
  - Major revision: if the approach is fundamentally flawed but the core problem is valid, you may redesign the approach entirely.
  - Pivot: if the reviewer's feedback reveals that the core problem itself is invalid (e.g., the gap no longer exists), you may propose a RELATED but substantially different idea that builds on the same research area. This is preferred over forcing a doomed idea to pass review.
- The output replaces the original idea (same tracking ID). Whether you make a small tweak or a full pivot, output a COMPLETE JSON object with ALL fields filled.
- In the output JSON, include a "change_type" field with one of: "minor", "major", or "pivot" to indicate the scope of your changes.
- Output the revised idea as a COMPLETE JSON object (same schema as original, plus "change_type").

## 停滞提醒
这个 idea 已经经过 4 轮修订，近 3 轮的平均分从 3.2 到 3.5，没有明显改善。

请认真思考：
- 当前方向是否存在根本性的瓶颈？反复的 minor fix 是否在回避核心问题？
- 如果你认为问题出在 approach 而非 framing，可以做 major revision。
- 如果你认为 core problem 本身就有问题（gap 不存在、问题不够重要），pivot 到同一研究领域下的新方向可能是更好的选择。
- 当然，如果你有信心这一轮修订能实现突破，继续改进也完全可以。

最终由你判断——做你认为最能提升 idea 质量的选择。

  "opportunity": "Test-time scaling is a dominant paradigm of 2025–26 ML: Large Language Monkeys (ICML 2024) showed coverage scales log-linearly with the number of samples over four orders of magnitude; the ICLR 2025 oral on optimal test-time compute (arXiv:2408.03314) demonstrates that training-free inference-time scaling can outperform parameter scaling on hard reasoning; and Table-R1 (EMNLP 2025) shows that structured tasks can benefit from test-time compute allocation — though Table-R1's inference-time gains require RL post-training (GRPO) before they emerge, making it a training+inference co-design result rather than a training-free precedent. The constrained decoding infrastructure now available (XGrammar is default in vLLM and SGLang as of March 2026, <40µs overhead) makes K=16–32 parallel samples feasible within the compute budget. A schema-aware aggregation function — span-overlap voting for entity boundaries, type plurality for classification, relation compatibility scoring — could be derived from schema structure alone and require no additional training. Crucially, whether the consistency signal is even actionable in the fine-tuned constrained-decoding regime (as opposed to hard-prompted models) is itself an open empirical question whose answer determines the entire viability of this research direction.   "landscape": "Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023) applies majority voting over reasoning chains for classification but has no principled extension to structured extraction spaces. Ranked Voting based Self-Consistency (ACL Findings 2025) extends self-consistency with Borda count and instant-runoff voting for open-ended QA — but still targets scalar answer spaces, not span-typed structured outputs. No published work has applied single-model K-sample aggregation with span-aware IoU clustering to any of these benchmarks, leaving this design space open.",
  "approach": "SpanVote is organized around two sequential research questions: RQ1 (calibration) and RQ2 (aggregation gains).\n\n**RQ1 — Does fine-tuned constrained-decoding produce actionable consistency signals?** On three primary benchmarks (ACE05, WikiEvents, RAMS), we generate K=16 hypotheses from a fine-tuned Qwen3-8B using XGrammar-constrained decoding and compute, for each predicted span: (a) the size of its IoU-compatible consensus cluster (how many of K outputs contain a matching span), and (b) its precision against gold annotation. Plotting calibration curves (cluster size vs. precision, binned) directly answers RQ1. If high-IoU-cluster spans are substantially more precise than singletons (e.g., cluster-of-8 precision ≥ cluster-of-1 precision + 10 F1 points), the consistency signal is actionable and justifies the aggregation framework. This finding is itself a primary contribution — it resolves the open question left by PMC2026 (which documented weak signals for hard-prompted K=5 models) and establishes fine-tuned constrained decoding as a qualitatively different regime. Reporting a negative result here (flat calibration curve) would also be a contribution: it would identify a failure mode of test-time consistency for IE.\n\n**Probabilistic motivation.** Span boundary noise in fine-tuned models is approximately Gaussian around the true boundary under temperature sampling: each sampled hypothesis perturbs start and end offsets by small random displacements, making median-offset aggregation statistically grounded analogously to RANSAC inlier averaging for geometric estimation. Type labels, conditioned on span boundaries, form a separate multinomial random variable — type plurality voting is the maximum-likelihood estimator of the type posterior under independent samples. Schema-enforced structural constraints (e.g., an event argument must fill a registered role) impose dependency between the span and type variables, which SpanVote's schema-aware scoring respects. This disentanglement — boundary noise ≈ Gaussian, type noise ≈ multinomial, structure = schema-constrained — is precisely why token-level majority voting fails: it conflates three structurally distinct random variables into a flat token sequence. **Boundary-noise appendix.** To ground the Gaussian framing empirically, we include an appendix figure reporting histograms of predicted-vs-gold span boundary offsets (start and end separately) on the ACE05 dev set under temperature sampling; if the empirical distribution is substantially non-Gaussian, the median-offset motivation is revised accordingly in the final paper.\n\n**RQ2 — SpanVote aggregation.** Conditioned on a positive calibration finding from RQ1, SpanVote applies schema-aware aggregation: (a) entity-mode for NER (IoU span clustering + type voting), (b) relation-mode adding directed pairwise entity-cluster compatibility, (c) EAE-mode adding hierarchical argument role constraints from the event schema. A full K ∈ {4, 8, 16, 32} × τ × strategy sweep is run on three primary benchmarks (ACE05, WikiEvents, RAMS) and the best configuration is transferred to five secondary benchmarks (Few-NERD, SciERC, TACRED/TACREV, DocRED, MAVEN).\n\n**BEMEAE secondary analysis.** On RAMS, SpanVote results are additionally reported under the BEMEAE metric (Fane et al., NAACL 2025), which uses deterministic + semantic matching and is calibrated against human judgments (BEMEAE-Human vs. BEMEAE-Best-Automated: τ = 0.94). BEMEAE was designed for RAMS and GENEVA; we extend it to WikiEvents as a secondary analysis, providing the first BEMEAE-metric EAE evaluation on WikiEvents. This validates whether SpanVote gains persist under a human-aligned evaluation standard, directly responding to BEMEAE's critique that ESM rankings disagree with human judgment (τ = 0.44 on RAMS).\n\n**RAMS metric specification.** All RAMS results target Arg-C Head F1 (argument classification with head word boundary matching), the standard metric used in post-2022 EAE literature, where SOTA is ~52–54 F1. Arg-C Coref F1 is reported as a secondary metric for comparability with papers (e.g., DeepStruct) that use it. All metrics are verified against the RAMS scorer v1.0c (March 2023 corrected release).\n\n**Compute.** Qwen3-8B on single A100-40GB; K=32 uses sequential K=16 mini-batches. Full sweep on three primary benchmarks (~190h A100), calibration analysis (~30h), transfer to five secondary benchmarks (~120h). Total ~340–380h A100 inference (excluding fine-tuning; see resource_estimate fine_tuning_note).",

The minimum is 0.20 (GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3), not 0.10. Additionally, the PMC paper used temperature=0.2 and top-p=0.1 (very conservative sampling suppressing output diversity) with only K=5 repetitions — these settings are themselves likely contributors to the weak signal and are a significant methodological distinction from SpanVote's constrained-decoding fine-tuned regime. Rephrase as a hypothesis to be validated: 'We hypothesize that τ=0.5 will recover ≥80% of per-dataset-optimal gains based on IoU threshold sensitivity patterns in related span-matching tasks, which we will validate via ablation.' This avoids overclaiming in what is a research proposal."]
Feedback: SpanVote has resolved every Round 3 issue cleanly — the EL4NER compute comparison is now honest and precise, the Table-R1 qualification is correct, the boundary-noise appendix is scoped, and the fine-tuning cost note is added. Three small fixes remain before this is submission-ready: (1) Fix the arithmetic on the compute budget. The current numbers add up to 202–222h H100, not ≤200H. The simplest fix is sharing fine-tuned checkpoints: ACE05 NER and RE use the same model checkpoint, TACRED/TACREV share one, reducing fine-tuning from 8 benchmarks × 8h A100 to approximately 5–6 distinct training runs × 8h = 40–48h A100 ≈ 20–24h H100. Combined with inference at 170–190h H100, the total becomes 190–214h H100 — still tight but defensible with the low estimate at 190h. Alternatively, drop K from 32 to 16 for the five secondary benchmarks (inference cost drops by ~30h A100 ≈ 15h H100, bringing the ceiling under 200H). (2) Correct the PMC citation: the range is r=0.20–0.30, not r=0.10–0.30. Add one sentence noting the PMC paper's conservative sampling settings (T=0.2, top-p=0.1, K=5) as an additional methodological distinction. (3) Reframe τ=0.5 ≥80% claim as a testable hypothesis rather than a known result. All three fixes are 1–2 sentence edits. After these corrections, the paper should be ready for EMNLP 2026 ARR submission targeting Findings; for Main consideration, a compelling positive calibration curve on ACE05 dev (cluster-of-8 precision vs. singleton clearly separated) would be the deciding factor.

# Summary of "The Sequential Edge" Paper

## Core Topic
This paper examines test-time scaling strategies for language model reasoning, comparing sequential refinement against parallel self-consistency approaches when compute budgets are equal.

## Main Findings

The researchers discovered that **sequential scaling outperforms parallel approaches** in the vast majority of cases:

- Sequential methods where "chains explicitly build upon previous attempts consistently outperforms the dominant parallel self-consistency paradigm in 95.6% of configurations"
- Accuracy improvements reached up to 46.7% in some configurations
- The authors introduce inverse-entropy weighted voting, a training-free technique that weights answers by the inverse entropy of their reasoning chains

## Applicability to Structured Tasks

**The paper does not address structured prediction or span extraction tasks.** The research focuses exclusively on reasoning benchmarks and general language model reasoning capabilities. These specialized structured tasks would require separate investigation to determine if the findings transfer.

## Key Challenge to Existing Practice

The work challenges the prevailing orthodoxy established by Wang et al.'s 2022 self-consistency decoding approach, arguing that "sequential refinement" should become "the robust default for modern LLM reasoning" rather than running independent parallel chains.
